title: Find the Nearest Clone
directAnswer: You want the fewest edges between any two nodes that share the target color. Because the graph is unweighted, BFS gives shortest distances. The clean answer is a multi-source BFS: seed the queue with every node of the target color, tag each node with the source it came from, and the first time two different sources' waves touch, that meeting distance is the global minimum. O(V + E).

remember.pattern: Multi-source BFS, meet-in-the-middle on same-color nodes
remember.formula:
seed queue with every node of target color, dist 0, tag source = self
BFS layer by layer:
    for neighbor v of u:
        if v unseen: source[v]=source[u]; dist[v]=dist[u]+1; enqueue
        elif source[v] != source[u]:        # waves from two clones met
            answer = min(answer, dist[u] + dist[v] + 1)
return answer or -1
rules: Two clones must be **distinct** nodes — a single node of the target color can never pair with itself, so fewer than two clones means `-1`.
The graph is **unweighted**, so BFS (not Dijkstra) gives shortest distances by counting edges in layers.
Tag each BFS node with the **source clone** it spread from; an answer appears only when two *different* sources collide.
BFS uses a queue and is naturally **iterative** — no recursion, so no stack overflow even at 10⁵ nodes.
Return `-1` when no two same-color nodes are connected — initialize the answer to infinity and check it at the end.
whenToUse: Shortest number of hops in an **unweighted** graph
Distance between any two members of a *set* of special nodes, not one fixed pair
You can start the search from many seeds at once and let the waves meet
Reachability plus hop-count, where all edges cost the same
antiSignals: Edges carry differing weights → Dijkstra, BFS layers no longer equal distance
You need the path between one fixed pair only → a single-source BFS is enough
You need every pairwise distance → BFS from each node (or Floyd-Warshall on small graphs)
remember.takeaway: Multi-source BFS turns 'closest pair among a set of nodes' into a single linear sweep: launch waves from all candidates simultaneously and the first collision between two different waves is your answer. The source tag is what makes one BFS replace many.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize an unweighted shortest-path question as BFS, and whether you can avoid the naive 'BFS from every clone' by collapsing it into one multi-source pass with source tagging.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Running BFS from each colored node separately (correct but O(C·(V+E))), or in the multi-source version recording a collision between two waves that trace back to the same source — which is not a real pair.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Seed all clones at once, carry a source label per node, and explain why the first inter-source collision is provably the global minimum because BFS expands in non-decreasing distance order.

problemStatement:
You are given an undirected, unweighted graph of `n` nodes (labeled `1` to `n`) described by two parallel edge lists `graphFrom` and `graphTo`. Each node `i` carries a color `ids[i]`.

Given a target color `val`, return the **minimum number of edges** on a path connecting two distinct nodes that both have color `val`. If fewer than two nodes have color `val`, or no two such nodes are connected, return `-1`.
constraints: The graph is undirected and may be disconnected
There may be 0, 1, or many nodes with the target color
understanding: Treat the nodes of the target color as a set of 'clones'. You need the shortest hop-count path between any two of them. Distances are measured in edges because the graph is unweighted, which makes BFS the right engine. Instead of measuring from each clone separately, you can launch the search from all clones at once and watch for the moment two separate search fronts — originating from two different clones — first touch.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are nodes 1-indexed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, HackerLand labels nodes 1..n. I will size arrays to n + 1 and ignore index 0, or shift to 0-based at the boundary.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can two clones be the same node?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. We need two distinct nodes of the target color. If only one node has the color, the answer is -1.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the graph weighted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — every edge counts as one hop. That is precisely why BFS, not Dijkstra, is correct.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could the two nearest clones be in different connected components?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Then they are unreachable from each other. If no connected pair exists, return -1.

examples.explanation: Nodes 1 and 4 both have color 1. Shortest path 1→2→4 is 2 edges. No closer pair exists.
Only node 2 has color 2. With fewer than two clones, there is no pair to connect.
Color-1 nodes are 1, 3, 5. Node 1 sits in component {1,2}, nodes 3 and 5 are in {3,4} and {5} — no two color-1 nodes share a component.

approaches.name: BFS from Each Clone (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: State this first — it is the obvious correct method. Run a separate BFS from every node of the target color, find the nearest other clone, and keep the global minimum.
hints: Forget cleverness: from one clone, what is the cheapest way to find the nearest other clone in an unweighted graph?
A BFS from a clone reaches nodes in increasing hop order. The first OTHER clone it pops is the nearest clone to that start.
Do that BFS from every clone and take the smallest distance found. C clones each cost one O(V + E) BFS.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each BFS visits every vertex and edge once → O(V + E). Running it from C clones gives O(C · (V + E)). When C is small this is near linear, but C can be as large as V, making it O(V·(V+E)) in the worst case.
approaches.explanation:
The most direct reading: for each clone, find its nearest fellow clone, then take the best across all clones.

**Why BFS and not DFS or Dijkstra.** The graph is unweighted, so the shortest path is the one with the fewest edges. BFS explores in concentric layers — all 1-hop nodes, then all 2-hop nodes, and so on — so the first time it reaches a target it has reached it by the shortest route. DFS does not have that layer property; Dijkstra would work but is overkill (and slower) when every edge weighs the same.

**Why the first other clone popped is the nearest.** Within a single BFS, nodes leave the queue in non-decreasing distance order. So the moment you pop a node that is a *different* clone of the same color, its recorded distance is the minimum distance from this start to any other clone. You can stop that BFS immediately.

**Why we must keep BFS iterative.** BFS is queue-driven, so it is already iterative — no recursion depth to blow even at `10⁵` nodes. (Contrast a recursive DFS, which would risk a stack overflow on a long chain.)

**Why this is the baseline, not the answer.** Repeating a full BFS from every clone repeats a lot of traversal. If half the graph shares the target color, you run `~V/2` BFS passes — quadratic. It is correct and easy to defend, but the multi-source version does the same job in one pass.
approaches.insight: A single BFS already answers 'nearest clone to *this* node'. The only inefficiency is repeating it; the optimal version removes the repetition by starting all the searches together.

pitfalls: Not stopping the BFS at the first other clone — wastes work, though still correct.
Re-using a single dist array across starts without resetting — stale distances corrupt later searches.
Forgetting the u != start guard — the start node itself has the target color and would falsely report distance 0.

approaches.name: Multi-Source BFS with Source Tags (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer to give. Seed the queue with every clone at once, tag each visited node with its originating clone, and the first collision between two different tags is the minimum.
hints: Instead of restarting BFS from each clone, what if all clones started spreading at the same instant?
Give each node a 'source' label = which clone's wave first reached it, plus its distance from that clone. Seed all clones at distance 0 with their own label.
When relaxing an edge u→v and v already belongs to a DIFFERENT source, the two waves have met: candidate = dist[u] + dist[v] + 1. The smallest such candidate is the answer.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single BFS touches each vertex and edge once → O(V + E). The source and distance arrays add O(V). Building the adjacency list is O(V + E). No factor of C — every clone is processed inside the one pass.
approaches.explanation:
The repetition in the baseline comes from launching `C` independent searches. Multi-source BFS launches them together and lets the fronts collide.

**Seeding and the source tag.** Put *every* clone into the queue at distance `0`, each labeled with itself as its source. As BFS proceeds, when a wave first reaches a node `v`, that node inherits the source of the wave that arrived. So `source[v]` answers 'which clone is closest to `v`', and `dist[v]` is that closest distance.

**Detecting a meeting.** Consider an edge `u → v`. If `v` is unseen, it joins `u`'s wave. But if `v` was *already* claimed by a **different** source, then the wave from `source[u]` and the wave from `source[v]` are about to overlap. A path runs `source[u] → … → u → v → … → source[v]` with length `dist[u] + 1 + dist[v]`. Every such collision yields a candidate distance between two distinct clones; the minimum over all collisions is the answer.

**Why the first collision found is essentially the smallest.** BFS dequeues nodes in non-decreasing distance order, so collisions surface roughly shortest-first. To be safe we do not stop at the very first collision — we take the `min` over all of them, because two collisions can be discovered in the same layer. That keeps the logic airtight while staying `O(V + E)`.

**Why same-source collisions are ignored.** If `source[u] == source[v]`, both nodes trace back to the *same* clone — connecting them does not join two distinct clones, so it is not a valid pair. The `source[u] != source[v]` guard is what enforces 'two distinct clones'.

**Why it stays iterative.** Like all BFS, the search runs off a queue with no recursion, so a graph of `10⁵` nodes never threatens the call stack.
approaches.insight: Tagging each node with the source that reached it first turns a set of independent BFS runs into one. The collision test `source[u] != source[v]` is the entire trick: it is how a single sweep discovers the closest pair across the whole set of clones.

code.python:
from collections import deque

def find_shortest(self, n: int, edges: list[list[int]], ids: list[int], val: int) -> int:
    adj: list[list[int]] = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)
        adj[v].append(u)
    source = [-1] * (n + 1)
    dist = [0] * (n + 1)
    queue = deque()
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        if ids[i - 1] == val:
            source[i] = i                   # each clone seeds its own wave
            queue.append(i)
    best = float('inf')
    while queue:
        u = queue.popleft()
        for v in adj[u]:
            if source[v] == -1:
                source[v] = source[u]
                dist[v] = dist[u] + 1
                queue.append(v)
            elif source[v] != source[u]:       # two waves meet
                best = min(best, dist[u] + dist[v] + 1)
    return -1 if best == float('inf') else best

edgeCases.input: ids has one node of color val
edgeCases.behavior: Only one seed enters the queue; no second wave ever exists, so no collision → best stays infinity → -1.
Their waves collide on the shared edge at dist 0 + 0 + 1 = 1 → answer 1.

pitfalls: Stopping at the first collision without taking a min — two collisions can occur in the same layer; keep the minimum.
Allowing same-source collisions to count — they connect a clone to itself, not two distinct clones.
Initializing dist to a sentinel that clashes with a real 0 distance — use the source array (-1) as the 'unseen' marker.
Using recursion instead of a queue — unnecessary and risks stack overflow; BFS is inherently iterative.

commonMistakes: Reaching for Dijkstra on an unweighted graph where plain BFS is correct and faster.
Reporting distance 0 by matching the start node against itself instead of a distinct clone.
In multi-source BFS, counting a collision between two nodes that trace back to the same source.
Forgetting the -1 case when fewer than two nodes carry the target color or none are connected.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Matching a node with itself
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The start node has the target color, so a check that does not exclude it reports a path of length 0 — but a clone cannot pair with itself.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if ids[u - 1] == val:
    best = min(best, dist[u])   # fires immediately on the start node
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if u != start and ids[u - 1] == val:
    best = min(best, dist[u])   # only a DIFFERENT clone counts

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Same-source collision in multi-source BFS
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If both endpoints of an edge trace to the same clone, joining them does not connect two distinct clones. Only an inter-source meeting is a valid pair.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Using Dijkstra on an unweighted graph
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Every edge costs the same here, so BFS already yields shortest hop counts in O(V + E). A min-heap adds a log factor and complexity for no benefit.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
import heapq
heap = [(0, start)]
while heap:
    d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)   # log factor wasted on equal weights
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
from collections import deque
queue = deque([start])
while queue:
    u = queue.popleft()          # plain BFS, O(V + E)

patternNote: Multi-Source BFS for Closest-Pair-in-a-Set. Recognize it when you need the shortest unweighted distance between any two members of a set of special nodes. Seed all of them, tag the source, and detect inter-source collisions. The same multi-source seeding powers Rotting Oranges and 01 Matrix.
